source.title: Label Noise in Adversarial Training: A Novel Perspective to Study Robust Overfitting
source.authors: Chengyu Dong; Liyuan Liu; Jing-Bo Shang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. There are minor OCR/formatting artifacts, but the relevant sections are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It experimentally tests epoch-wise double descent in adversarial training, a training setting distinct from the standard-training setting discussed in the original work.
record.gate_note: The paper directly studies epoch-wise test-error curves and how they vary with model width, perturbation radius, data quality, architecture, and learning-rate schedule. Cited findings from other papers are not recorded as results. The calibration method's results on other datasets are summarized in rows only where the paper reports endpoint overfitting measurements bearing on epoch-wise behavior.
record.test_reason: The study trains adversarially (PGD) for 1,000 epochs on CIFAR-10 and reports epoch-wise robust test-error curves showing a second descent after robust overfitting. It varies model width, architecture, learning-rate schedule, perturbation radius and data quality. It also compares adversarially augmented and Gaussian-augmented fixed training sets to tie the peak to (implicit) label noise. Adversarial training is a new setting for the epoch-wise claim (V2) and the noise-dependence claim (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that inheriting clean labels for adversarial examples introduces implicit label noise, which explains robust overfitting and its dependence on perturbation radius and data quality. They conclude that robust overfitting is the early part of an epoch-wise double descent seen with much longer training, whose model-size pattern matches standard training. They also propose calibrated self-distillation labels (KD-AT-Auto) that mitigate robust overfitting without manual tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines epoch-wise error curves under adversarial training and controlled perturbation/data-quality settings, rather than reproducing the original standard-training experiments or their model-size and sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported epoch-wise curve varies with model width and architecture, perturbation radius, data quality, and learning-rate schedule. The second descent may be delayed for VGG-11 and under piecewise decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on calibrated self-distillation labels (KD-AT-Auto) reduces the best-last robust-accuracy gap to under 0.5 points on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny-ImageNet, vs 1.8–5.9 for AT, over 80–160 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacing inherited labels with calibrated model probabilities removes robust overfitting (the first rise of epoch-wise double descent) in adversarial training.

record.problems: Several relevant curves are figure-only, without numerical values or reported uncertainty. The 5k training subset is used for extended epoch analyses. The tabled best/last checkpoint comparisons show endpoint gaps, not full epoch-wise trajectories. The paper's data-quality and perturbation-radius results support its explanation but do not directly quantify the latent label noise in each plotted condition.
record.rows_left_out: No directly relevant plotted model, schedule, perturbation-radius, or data-quality conditions were omitted. The many tables on additional architectures, adversarial-training methods, attacks, and added teachers report best/last performance for the proposed calibration method rather than full epoch-wise curves; they were not separately extracted as evidence for the double-descent shape.

untested.parts: Standard-training epoch-wise double descent on real data with explicit label noise; uncertainty across seeds; numeric locations or heights of the peak.

Multiple/triple descent; whether the peak disappears under optimally tuned regularization (weight decay is off); direct measurement of label-noise rates per condition (noise is inferred theoretically); per-radius ordering of Figure 5 curves.
No model-size sweep at a fixed epoch; only three widths are compared as epoch curves.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V2 'challenges' label was wrong. Small/medium-model absence and no-noise controls mirror the original's own conditions (sufficient size, label noise needed); they qualify scope rather than contradict. Clean/Gaussian controls are recoded as V6 evidence. The Table 1 KD rows are the study's own method and are unlinked. Double-descent analyses use 5k subsets for the fixed-data and radius/quality experiments, single runs, and no error bars in the figures. Label noise is derived theoretically (lower bounds), not measured.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error sweep across model sizes at a fixed training stage, with a peak near the training-set interpolation threshold.
The experiments concern robust error in adversarial training and do not establish the epoch-wise curve for standard training generally. Some results are plots without reported numerical values.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold to test whether more samples raise test error.
No comparison across general model classes establishing a capacity-wise curve beyond the interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting the peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

The paper examines epoch-wise behavior in relation to perturbation radius, data quality, and its label-noise account. It does not test multiple or triple descent, or whether the peak disappears under optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective parameter measure or test of whether that converts the curve to an ordinary U-shape.
